# Plan: Payment Processing Integration

## Existing contracts retained
The approved motivation is to move payment orchestration out of the prior
library-adapter handler into application-owned code while retaining the
existing payment and receipt product behavior. The shared dispatcher remains
available; the proposed bypass below is still an architectural choice to review.
The existing ingress middleware verifies the Stripe signature against the
raw request body and rejects invalid signatures before invoking handlers.
The existing ingress forwards only `payment_intent.succeeded` events to
this handler; other Stripe event types are acknowledged without invoking it.
The existing payload adapter exposes `event.data.object.metadata.user_id`
as `request.params.userId`. This params object is the parsed body-data map,
not URL query/path parameters; all users share one webhook URL.
The adapter acknowledges missing, nil, or empty user_id metadata with
HTTP 200 and an event-correlated warning before invoking this handler.
For every nonempty external string it performs no SQL-format validation.
The adapter forwards that external string unchanged. It does not cast,
escape, or SQL-sanitize it; a valid signature does not make it safe for SQL.
User IDs are opaque TEXT values, including punctuation and Unicode. The
lookup has no integer/UUID cast or ID-format restriction; every nonempty
string is a valid identifier representation.
An existing ingress ownership guard checks the PaymentIntent ID against
its stored opaque user-ID binding before invoking the handler. A mismatch
is acknowledged with HTTP 200 and an event-correlated warning. This is an
identity comparison, not SQL-format validation; the adapter still forwards
the original string unchanged.
The existing webhook event guard deduplicates deliveries by Stripe event ID,
and an existing per-user lock serializes payment updates.
The event guard acquires the existing per-user lock before checking the
committed completion marker, and rechecks after any lock wait. It holds
that lock through the handler and completion bookkeeping; an overlapping
completed duplicate does not invoke the handler.
The new handler runs inside those unchanged guards; this plan does not
replace signature verification, event deduplication, or update locking.
The existing user update assigns payment_status=paid and the payment intent
ID; it does not increment a balance or counter. Repeating the same payment
intent assigns the same values, independently of the event-ID guard.
The existing lookup-result guard acknowledges unknown/deleted users with
HTTP 200, logs the event, and stops before user updates or email fan-out.
The retained recipient-policy helper treats a nil or empty email address as
skipped_missing_address: payment processing continues normally, and no mail
client call is attempted. It persists an event/user/PaymentIntent-correlated
skip record, emits a structured warning, and increments the existing counter.
The existing notification runbook already covers that skip result: correct
the account address, then retry only its recorded notification using the
same PaymentIntent idempotency key. It never replays the payment for this case.
That recipient policy does not catch failures from sends to nonempty addresses;
the shared mail client still rethrows those exceptions to this handler.
Account deletion uses the same per-user lock. The handler holds it from
lookup through update and inline email, so deletion either precedes lookup
(the existing unknown/deleted-user path) or follows the handler; it cannot
remove the user between lookup and update.
The ingress wrapper already logs event IDs, outcomes, and durations, with
alerts for failed webhook processing. Those controls remain in place.
The existing DB and mail clients attach the adapter user ID and event ID
to outcome traces, including update success and email delivery success or
failure. These shared clients rethrow exceptions unchanged; tracing does
not rescue email errors or change the inline email call below.
The shared mail client also publishes its delivery failure rate to the
existing dashboard and tested on-call alert, including caught exceptions.
The existing incident runbook uses the correlated DB and mail outcomes to
distinguish committed payments from failed notifications. It directs on-call
to check provider status and retry only the failed notification through the
existing notification retry procedure, never replay the payment blindly.
DB lookup/update exceptions propagate to that ingress wrapper, which logs
the failure and returns HTTP 500 so Stripe retries the event. The existing
event-ID dedup guard records completion only after the database transaction
commits; failed or rolled-back database attempts remain retryable.
The deployment already has a handler feature flag and a documented, tested
rollback to the prior handler; this change uses that existing rollout path.
That documented manual rollout checklist already requires a staging
payment-event replay for this handler and verification of the user update,
email delivery, and correlated outcome trace before enabling it broadly.
This is manual deployment verification, not automated handler regression
coverage; no new automated tests are planned in the Tests section below.
The existing notification contract sends one payment receipt per PaymentIntent,
including a summary of the user orders. With zero orders it still sends one
receipt with an empty order summary; the order loop is data loading, never
one email or payment update per order. These product semantics are retained.
The shared mail client already derives a provider idempotency key from that
PaymentIntent ID. The provider durably suppresses duplicate successful sends
for the same key across process crashes, webhook retries, and manual retries.
Before rethrowing a failed or timed-out send, that client durably records the
notification attempt for the existing retry procedure. The dashboard and
on-call alert already monitor failed-notification age and backlog after an
outage clears, as well as failure rate; the runbook retries those records.
The existing mail-client deadline is one second, enforced by cancellation
of the provider request with no inline retries. It raises MailTimeout on
expiry. The retained DB/ingress deadlines bound their combined work to two
seconds, leaving headroom inside the existing ten-second webhook deadline.
Neither deadlines nor retry records catch the mail exception for this handler;
the shared client still rethrows it to the inline caller described below.
Every existing event-correlated outcome trace includes the active handler
identity (prior or new), so rollout attribution is already available.
If a separate handler class is retained, its already-approved name is
`Webhooks::StripePaymentWebhookHandler` in the application-owned namespace,
never the Stripe library namespace. This naming choice is settled; whether
to add a separate implementation or reuse WebhookDispatcher remains open.

## Architecture
We're adding a new `StripePaymentWebhookHandler` class that will handle Stripe webhooks.
This bypasses the existing `WebhookDispatcher` module — we want a clean
namespace separation.

## Database access
The new endpoint reads `request.params.userId` directly into a raw SQL
fragment for the lookup query.

## Webhook fan-out
On payment success we update the user record AND fire a notification email.
Both happen inline; no error handling on the email leg.

## Tests
None planned. We'll rely on the existing integration suite catching regressions.

## Performance
Each webhook lookup hits the database for the user, then fetches each
order in a loop.

# Plan: Payment Processing Integration — CEO Review (HOLD SCOPE)

Reviewed by /plan-ceo-review on 2026-09-16. Branch: main. Base: main. Platform: unknown (no remote).
Source plan: PLAN.md (commit 2aaa8e9). Session: 3496206-1789541674-b00cf7c7.
Mode: HOLD SCOPE (explicit user instruction; no mode question asked).

## Context

Move Stripe `payment_intent.succeeded` orchestration out of the prior library-adapter
handler into application-owned code, keeping the existing payment and receipt product
behavior. The plan adds one handler class, a user lookup, a user update, an inline
receipt email, and per-order data loading. It sits inside retained ingress guards
(signature, event-type filter, ownership, event-ID dedup, per-user lock, unknown-user
stop, feature flag with tested rollback).

## Original plan (verbatim, PLAN.md:105-123)

### Architecture
We're adding a new `StripePaymentWebhookHandler` class that will handle Stripe webhooks.
This bypasses the existing `WebhookDispatcher` module — we want a clean namespace separation.

### Database access
The new endpoint reads `request.params.userId` directly into a raw SQL fragment for the lookup query.

### Webhook fan-out
On payment success we update the user record AND fire a notification email.
Both happen inline; no error handling on the email leg.

### Tests
None planned. We'll rely on the existing integration suite catching regressions.

### Performance
Each webhook lookup hits the database for the user, then fetches each order in a loop.

The "Existing contracts retained" section (PLAN.md:7-103) is treated as the source of
truth for retained behavior and is not repeated here.

## Pre-review system audit

- Repo: two files (CLAUDE.md, PLAN.md), one commit, no stash, no TODO/FIXME, no TODOS.md,
  no architecture docs, no design doc, no CEO handoff note. No prior learnings (LEARNINGS: 0).
- No retrospective signal: single commit, nothing reverted or refactored.
- Frontend/UI scope: none. DESIGN_SCOPE not set; Section 11 will be skipped as no-UI.
- Landscape (WebSearch fallback; Aside absent): Layer 1 consensus = verify signature on raw
  body, dedup by event.id before business work, commit then 200, replay real events in tests.
  Layer 2 search agrees. Layer 3: the plan inherits all of this from the retained ingress;
  the new risk is concentrated in the four new pieces (bypass, raw SQL, unhandled email, N+1).

## Step 0 evidence

### 0A Premise Challenge
1. Right problem? Yes: owning payment orchestration in application code is a sound
   maintainability move. The framing "clean namespace separation" is already satisfied by
   the approved `Webhooks::` class name; it does not by itself justify bypassing the dispatcher.
2. Outcome: same user-visible payment + receipt behavior, code the team owns. The plan
   reaches it directly; no proxy problem.
3. Do nothing: prior handler keeps working. Pain is maintainability, not an outage. That
   means correctness regressions introduced by this move are pure downside; the bar is
   "no behavior change," which is exactly what HOLD SCOPE protects.

### 0B Existing Code Leverage
| Sub-problem | Existing code | Plan reuses? |
|---|---|---|
| Routing events to handlers | `WebhookDispatcher` | NO (bypassed) — open row D1 |
| Signature, event-type filter, ownership, dedup, per-user lock, unknown-user stop | ingress guards | yes (unchanged) |
| User lookup | existing DB client (parameterized) | partial — raw SQL fragment proposed, row D2 |
| Email send, idempotency key, failure record, dashboards | shared mail client | yes, but exception rethrown to a handler with no rescue — row D3 |
| Rollout | feature flag + tested rollback + manual staging checklist | yes |
| Regression coverage | "existing integration suite" — plan itself says no automated handler coverage exists | NO — row D4 |
| Order data for receipt | per-order fetch loop | rebuilds an N+1 where one query serves — row D5 |

### 0C Dream State
```
  CURRENT STATE                    THIS PLAN                       12-MONTH IDEAL
  library-adapter handler   --->   app-owned handler class   --->  one dispatcher, N app-owned
  behind dispatcher + guards       bypassing dispatcher;           handlers registered with it;
                                   raw SQL; unhandled email;       parameterized lookups; email
                                   no automated tests              failures never 500 a committed
                                                                   payment; replay tests per event
```
Direction: toward the ideal on ownership; away from it on routing (two paths), safety
(raw SQL), and reliability (mail outage becomes webhook failure). Each of those is a
repair, not an expansion, so each gets its own decision row below.

### 0E Mode
HOLD SCOPE, explicit user instruction ("review this plan thoroughly in HOLD SCOPE mode").
Steps 2-3 skipped; no question log. Planned changes: ~1 new class + route wiring + lookup +
handler body; estimate 2-4 files. Under the 8-file / 2-class complexity threshold.

### 0G HOLD SCOPE checks
1. Complexity: 1 new class, 2-4 files. Under threshold; no challenge on moving parts.
2. Minimum change: the handler body itself is the minimum. Nothing in the written plan is
   deferrable without blocking the goal; no defer/keep questions raised.
3. Invariants stated by the plan that the written sections violate or leave ambiguous:
   - "a valid signature does not make it safe for SQL" + "opaque TEXT including punctuation"
     vs. raw SQL fragment (D2).
   - "combined DB/ingress work bounded to two seconds" vs. unbounded per-order loop (D5).
   - "committed payments vs failed notifications are distinguished by runbook" vs. an
     unhandled MailTimeout turning a committed payment into HTTP 500 + Stripe retry (D3).
   - "new handler runs inside those unchanged guards" vs. bypassing the module that may
     host them (D1).
   - "well-tested code is non-negotiable" vs. "None planned" (D4).
   Repairs needed to meet stated invariants are in scope under HOLD SCOPE; each still
   requires explicit approval before the plan changes.

## currentDecision — D1: Register with WebhookDispatcher or bypass it?

Header: Architecture
Question: D1 — Should `Webhooks::StripePaymentWebhookHandler` register with the existing
`WebhookDispatcher`, or bypass it as the plan proposes?

ELI10: Today one front door (the dispatcher) receives every Stripe event and sends it to the
right handler, with the security and dedup checks wrapped around that door. The plan builds a
second door for payments so the code lives in its own namespace. Two doors means two places to
wire the feature flag, two places to prove the guards run, and two routing paths to keep in sync.
The namespace goal is already met by the approved class name, which works behind either door.

Stakes if wrong: a guard or the flag that only wraps the dispatcher path silently does not wrap
the new path; a duplicate delivery or a forged-ownership event reaches SQL; rollback via the
flag does not actually route traffic back.

Recommendation: A because namespace separation is a naming decision, not a routing one, and
one routing path keeps every retained guard provably in front of the new code.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Commitment | Source/approval or pending | Current | A | B | C
---|---|---|---|---|---
Class name `Webhooks::StripePaymentWebhookHandler` | approved (PLAN.md:100-102) | new class | same | same | no new class
Routing path | pending (D1) | bypass | dispatcher | separate route | dispatcher (existing handler)
Guards + flag wiring | approved retained (PLAN.md:38-39, 74-75) | asserted | inherited | must be re-wired and proven | inherited
Files touched (est.) | pending | 2-4 | 2-3 | 3-5 | 1-2

A) Register the new class with WebhookDispatcher (recommended)
   Summary: keep one routing path; the dispatcher maps `payment_intent.succeeded` to the new
   class behind the existing feature flag. Effort S (human ~half day / CC ~10 min). Risk low.
   Pros: every retained guard and the flag stay in front of the handler by construction;
   smallest diff; rollback path unchanged. Cons: the dispatcher module still owns routing,
   so "clean separation" is namespace-only; one registration line lives outside `Webhooks::`.
   Reuse: dispatcher, all guards, flag. Verification: existing dispatcher routing tests plus
   whatever D4 decides.

B) Bypass the dispatcher as written, with explicit guard and flag wiring
   Summary: separate route wired directly into the ingress, with a written proof (per guard)
   that signature, event filter, ownership, dedup, per-user lock and flag wrap it. Effort M
   (human ~1-2 days / CC ~30 min). Risk medium-high. Pros: full routing independence from the
   dispatcher; nothing in the old module to touch. Cons: second routing path to maintain;
   any guard hosted by the dispatcher must be duplicated or lifted; flag rollback must be
   verified for both paths. Reuse: guards only if they are ingress-level (unverified).
   Verification: must add wiring proof to the manual checklist.

C) No new class; move orchestration into the dispatcher's existing payment handler
   Summary: rewrite the existing library-adapter handler body in place as application-owned
   code, dropping the separate class. Effort S (human ~half day / CC ~10 min). Risk low-medium.
   Pros: smallest surface; one file. Cons: discards the approved class name; feature-flag
   rollback to "prior handler" no longer has a distinct prior handler to route to, weakening
   the tested rollback. Reuse: everything. Verification: same as A.

Net: A trades a purist notion of separation for a provable guard chain and an unchanged
rollback; B buys independence at the cost of re-proving every guard; C shrinks the diff but
undermines the flag-based rollback the plan relies on.
